opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing papers leave out is the mess. A published paper is a beautifully cleaned-up narrative. You read it and it goes: we had this hypothesis, we designed this elegant experiment, we got this result, and here's the conclusion. It reads like a straight line. But anyone who's actually been at the bench knows it's nothing like that. It's a random walk with a lot of dead ends, and the story gets written backwards once you know where you ended up.

Papers also leave out how much of discovery is driven by tools and technique, the unglamorous stuff. Somebody figured out how to get a protocol to work reliably. Someone spent six months optimizing a delivery method, or noticed a weird band on a gel that everyone else would have thrown away. That tacit knowledge, the hands-on craft, almost never makes it into the methods section. Honestly, the methods section is often the least reproducible part of the paper, which is ironic, because it's supposed to be the recipe.

And then there's the human side: who talked to whom at a conference, which postdoc had a hunch at 2 a.m., which collaboration happened because two people shared a lab bay. A lot of breakthroughs come from those collisions. They come from people bringing a technique from one field into another where nobody thought to use it. The formal literature strips all of that out because it isn't "data."

Then there's the negative space. All the experiments that didn't work, all the reagents that failed, the hypotheses we were confident about that turned out to be wrong. That's a huge amount of information, and it basically disappears. Every lab ends up rediscovering the same failures independently. If you think about it from a machine learning perspective, we're training the whole field on a heavily biased dataset made only of positive results, written as post-hoc rationalizations. That's part of why I'm excited about building systems that capture the full experimental process, including the failures and the iteration, because that's where a lot of the real learning actually lives.

r001.rationale: The response describes bench work as “a random walk with a lot of dead ends,” conveying experimental trial and error.

r002.rationale: It says failed experiments, reagents, and hypotheses “basically disappear” from published accounts.

r003.rationale: It says papers present discovery as a “straight line” and describes the story as written backwards after the outcome is known.

r004.rationale: It frames published results as a biased dataset from a machine-learning perspective, then connects capturing failures and iteration to where useful learning lives.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest thing papers leave out is the sequencing of the process. A paper is written backwards. You start from the conclusion, and then you construct this clean, linear narrative where hypothesis leads to experiment leads to result. But that's almost never how it happened. In reality, you were stumbling around in the dark for eighteen months, the key experiment was often an accident or a control that behaved strangely, and the hypothesis in the introduction was frequently written after you already knew the answer.

The second thing is the failure rate. For every figure in a paper, there are maybe twenty or fifty experiments that didn't work, and most of those failures are technical rather than conceptual. The reagent was bad, the cells were unhappy, someone didn't optimize the protocol. That tacit knowledge, the hands-on craft of getting a system to actually work in your lab, is almost completely absent from the methods section. It lives in people's notebooks and in conversations at the bench. That's why the best way to learn a technique is still to go visit the lab that developed it, rather than reading about it.

And the third thing, which I think matters a lot for how we think about AI in science, is that papers hide how much of discovery is taste. Deciding which problem to work on, which weird result to chase versus ignore, when to abandon a direction. Those judgment calls are where most of the value is created, and they're invisible in the final product. If you only train on the literature, you're training on the sanitized output, not on the process that generated it. So I'm genuinely interested in how we capture the messy, iterative, often embarrassing part of science, because that's where the real signal is.

r001.rationale: It describes researchers as “stumbling around in the dark,” with accidental discoveries and many experiments that did not work, conveying trial and error.

r002.rationale: It says failed experiments and the tacit knowledge around them are almost completely absent from papers and methods sections.

r003.rationale: It says papers present a “clean, linear narrative” from hypothesis to experiment to result, although that is almost never how discovery happened.

r004.rationale: It links capturing the messy research process to AI in science, explaining that training only on published literature gives AI the sanitized output rather than the process that generated it.

astra-6.text:
I think they leave out a lot of the uncertainty. A paper presents a clean sequence: here was the question, here was the experiment, here was the result. But when you’re doing the work, you don’t know which observation is important or even whether you’re asking the right question. You’re trying to distinguish something interesting from something that just went wrong.

And the path between those things is often social. Someone looks at your data and offers a different interpretation. A conversation changes the experiment you were going to do next. Those moments are hard to capture in a figure legend, but they can change the direction of a project.

You need a coherent story to communicate a discovery. But that coherence is retrospective. What gets lost is how much of discovery involves being confused—and figuring out which part of that confusion is worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty and sorting meaningful observations from things that went wrong, but does not characterize experimental biology as trial and error.

r002.rationale: It says confusion and changes of direction are hard to capture, but does not identify failed attempts as information omitted from published accounts.

r003.rationale: It contrasts papers’ clean sequence with the messy process of discovery, but does not say papers portray discovery as an inexorable logical progression.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect records of the research process to their usefulness for AI reasoning models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they leave out a lot of the uncertainty. A paper presents a clean sequence: here was the question, here was the experiment, here was the result. But when you’re doing the work, you often don’t know whether you’re asking the right question, whether your assay is working, or whether the weird result is an artifact or the most interesting thing you’ve seen.

And the path is much more social than the paper conveys. Somebody makes an offhand comment, you talk through a confusing result with a colleague, or someone from another field gives you a different way to think about it. Those interactions can change the direction of a project, but they’re hard to capture in a figure legend.

What gets lost is the judgment involved: which surprises to follow, which failures to troubleshoot, and when to abandon an assumption. Once you know the answer, the path looks much more obvious than it felt at the time.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty, surprises, failures, and troubleshooting, but does not characterize experimental biology as trial and error.

r002.rationale: It says papers leave out uncertainty and that the judgment involved in handling failures gets lost, but does not clearly identify failed attempts themselves as missing from published accounts.

r003.rationale: The response says papers present a clean question-to-experiment-to-result sequence and make the path look more obvious in retrospect, conveying a falsely orderly progression.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect records of the research process to their usefulness for AI reasoning models.
